topics.title: Microeconomics & Market Structures
topics.description: How households and firms make choices under scarcity, how prices form in markets, and how competition, monopoly and oligopoly change prices, output and welfare.

modules.title: Supply, demand and equilibrium
modules.summary: Build the core market model and use it to predict how prices and quantities respond to shocks.

lessons.title: Scarcity and opportunity cost
lessons.summary: Every choice gives something up; the opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone.
lessons.body:
Economics starts from scarcity: wants are unlimited, but time, money and resources are not. Because of this, every choice has an opportunity cost, which is the value of the next best alternative you give up. It is not the sum of all alternatives, only the best one.

Example: a student can spend Saturday working a shift that pays 150,000 UZS or studying for an exam. If she studies, the opportunity cost of studying is the 150,000 UZS of lost wages, plus anything else she would have valued from the shift. A production possibilities frontier (PPF) draws the same idea for a whole economy: moving along the curve to make more of one good means making less of another, and the slope of the PPF is the opportunity cost.

Key takeaway: costs in economics are measured in what you give up, not only in what you pay. A rational decision compares the benefit of an option with its full opportunity cost.

lessons.title: Demand and the law of demand
lessons.summary: Why quantity demanded falls as price rises, and the difference between a movement along and a shift of the demand curve.
lessons.body:
The law of demand says that, other things equal, a higher price lowers the quantity demanded. A demand curve plots price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis and slopes downward. A linear example is Qd = 100 − 2P: at P = 10 buyers want 80 units, at P = 20 they want 60.

It is essential to separate two kinds of change. A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve (a change in quantity demanded). A change in anything else shifts the whole curve (a change in demand). The main shifters are income (demand for normal goods rises with income, for inferior goods it falls), prices of substitutes and complements, tastes, expectations about future prices, and the number of buyers.

Key takeaway: price moves you along the demand curve; income, related prices, tastes, expectations and population shift it. Mixing the two is the most common mistake in market analysis.

lessons.title: Supply and market equilibrium
lessons.summary: How the supply curve is built from producers’ costs and where supply and demand meet.
lessons.body:
The law of supply says that a higher price raises the quantity firms are willing to sell, because higher prices cover the higher cost of producing extra units. Supply shifts when input costs, technology, taxes, the number of sellers or expectations change.

Equilibrium is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. With Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = −20 + 4P, set them equal: 100 − 2P = −20 + 4P, so 6P = 120 and P* = 20. Then Q* = 100 − 40 = 60 units. Above 20 there is a surplus that pushes the price down; below 20 there is a shortage that pushes it up.

Comparative statics means comparing equilibria before and after a shock. If a drought raises costs, supply shifts left: price rises and quantity falls. If incomes rise for a normal good, demand shifts right: both price and quantity rise. When both curves shift at once, one of the two outcomes is ambiguous and depends on the size of each shift.

Key takeaway: solve Qd = Qs for the equilibrium price, then substitute back for quantity. To predict a shock, decide which curve moves, in which direction, and read the new intersection.

lessons.title: Price elasticity of demand
lessons.summary: Measuring how strongly buyers react to price changes and what that means for revenue.
lessons.body:
Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to price: Ed = (% change in quantity) ÷ (% change in price). Using the midpoint method avoids getting a different answer depending on direction: %ΔQ = ΔQ ÷ average Q.

Example: when a café raises the price of coffee from 10,000 to 12,000 UZS, daily sales fall from 220 to 180 cups. %ΔQ = −40 ÷ 200 = −20%, %ΔP = 2,000 ÷ 11,000 ≈ 18.2%, so |Ed| ≈ 1.1. Demand is elastic (|Ed| > 1) when buyers react strongly, inelastic (|Ed| < 1) when they barely react, and unit elastic at exactly 1.

Elasticity determines what happens to total revenue (P × Q). If demand is elastic, a price increase lowers revenue; if it is inelastic, a price increase raises revenue. Demand is more elastic when close substitutes exist, when the good is a large share of the budget, when it is a luxury, and over longer time horizons.

Key takeaway: before changing a price, estimate elasticity. Inelastic demand means a price rise increases revenue; elastic demand means it reduces revenue.

modules.title: Consumer choice and welfare
modules.summary: Utility, budget constraints and how markets create surplus for buyers and sellers.

lessons.title: Utility and diminishing marginal utility
lessons.summary: Consumers get less extra satisfaction from each additional unit of a good.
lessons.body:
Utility is a way of ranking how much satisfaction a bundle of goods gives. What matters for decisions is marginal utility (MU): the extra utility from one more unit. For most goods marginal utility diminishes: the first glass of water on a hot day is worth a lot, the fifth much less.

A consumer spends wisely when the last som spent on each good gives the same extra satisfaction. This is the equal marginal principle: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If MUx ÷ Px is higher, moving spending from y to x raises total utility, and diminishing marginal utility guarantees the ratios eventually equalize.

Example: bread costs 4,000 UZS and gives MU = 20 for the next loaf (5 per 1,000 UZS); tea costs 10,000 UZS and gives MU = 30 (3 per 1,000 UZS). The consumer should buy more bread and less tea until the ratios match.

Key takeaway: decisions are made at the margin. Diminishing marginal utility is the behavioral reason demand curves slope downward.

lessons.title: Budget constraints and optimal choice
lessons.summary: The budget line shows what a consumer can afford; the best bundle is where it touches the highest indifference curve.
lessons.body:
A budget constraint lists every bundle a consumer can afford: Px·X + Py·Y = I, where I is income. Drawn with X on the horizontal axis, the budget line has slope −Px ÷ Py, the market rate at which one good trades for the other. A rise in income shifts the line out in parallel; a rise in the price of X rotates it inward along the X axis.

Preferences are drawn as indifference curves, each joining bundles the consumer likes equally. Their slope is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS = MUx ÷ MUy), the rate at which the consumer is willing to trade. The optimum is the tangency point where MRS = Px ÷ Py: willingness to trade equals the market price ratio.

Example: with income 100,000 UZS, Px = 10,000 and Py = 5,000, the consumer can buy at most 10 units of X or 20 units of Y. A price cut on X both makes X relatively cheaper (substitution effect) and raises real purchasing power (income effect).

Key takeaway: optimal choice combines what you can afford (budget line) with what you prefer (indifference curves). Every price change has a substitution effect and an income effect.

lessons.title: Consumer surplus, producer surplus and deadweight loss
lessons.summary: Measuring the gains from trade and the losses caused by taxes and price controls.
lessons.body:
Consumer surplus is the difference between what buyers are willing to pay and what they actually pay; on a graph it is the area below the demand curve and above the price. Producer surplus is the difference between the price sellers receive and their minimum acceptable price; it is the area above the supply curve and below the price. Their sum is total surplus, the economic value a market creates.

Example: with Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = −20 + 4P, equilibrium is P* = 20, Q* = 60. Demand hits zero quantity at P = 50, so consumer surplus = ½ × 60 × (50 − 20) = 900. Supply starts at P = 5, so producer surplus = ½ × 60 × (20 − 5) = 450. Total surplus is 1,350.

A competitive equilibrium maximizes total surplus. Taxes, price ceilings and price floors push quantity away from Q*, and the value of trades that no longer happen is the deadweight loss, a triangle between the curves. A rent ceiling below equilibrium, for example, creates a shortage and a deadweight loss even though some renters gain.

Key takeaway: surplus measures who gains from a market. Interventions that move quantity away from equilibrium create deadweight loss, a pure loss to society.

modules.title: Production and costs
modules.summary: How firms turn inputs into output and how costs behave in the short and long run.

lessons.title: Production functions and diminishing returns
lessons.summary: Output depends on inputs, and adding more of one input eventually adds less output.
lessons.body:
A production function shows the maximum output a firm can make from given inputs, often written Q = f(L, K) for labor and capital. In the short run at least one input, usually capital, is fixed. The marginal product of labor (MPL) is the extra output from one more worker.

The law of diminishing marginal returns says that if you keep adding workers to a fixed amount of capital, MPL eventually falls. A bakery with two ovens might see output rise from 100 to 180 loaves when a second baker joins, but only to 220 with a third, because the bakers start waiting for oven space.

A common functional form is Cobb-Douglas: Q = A·L^a·K^b. If a + b = 1 there are constant returns to scale (doubling all inputs doubles output); a + b > 1 means increasing returns, and a + b < 1 decreasing returns. Returns to scale describe the long run, when every input can change; diminishing returns describe the short run.

Key takeaway: diminishing marginal returns is a short-run idea with one input fixed. Returns to scale is a long-run idea about scaling all inputs together.

lessons.title: Fixed, variable, marginal and average costs
lessons.summary: The cost curves every firm uses to decide how much to produce.
lessons.body:
Total cost splits into fixed cost (FC), which does not change with output, such as rent, and variable cost (VC), which does, such as flour and hourly wages: TC = FC + VC. Dividing by output gives average fixed cost, average variable cost and average total cost: ATC = TC ÷ Q.

Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit: MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ, or the derivative dTC/dQ. Because of diminishing returns, MC eventually rises, which makes the ATC curve U-shaped. MC always crosses ATC and AVC at their minimum points: when the marginal unit costs less than the average it pulls the average down, and when it costs more it pulls the average up.

Example: TC = 500 + 10Q + Q². Fixed cost is 500 and MC = 10 + 2Q. ATC = 500/Q + 10 + Q is minimized where MC = ATC: 10 + 2Q = 500/Q + 10 + Q, so Q² = 500 and Q ≈ 22.4 units.

Key takeaway: marginal cost drives production decisions; average cost tells you whether the firm makes a profit. MC crosses ATC at its lowest point.

lessons.title: Long-run costs and economies of scale
lessons.summary: Why average costs fall as some firms grow, and why they rise when firms get too large.
lessons.body:
In the long run a firm can choose its plant size, so every cost is variable. The long-run average cost (LRAC) curve traces the lowest average cost achievable at each output level when the firm picks the best plant for that output.

Economies of scale occur when LRAC falls as output grows. Sources include specialization of workers, spreading large fixed investments such as software or factories over more units, and bulk purchasing discounts. Diseconomies of scale occur when LRAC rises because coordination becomes harder and management layers multiply. Between them is often a flat range of constant returns.

The minimum efficient scale (MES) is the smallest output at which LRAC reaches its minimum. If MES is large relative to market demand, as in electricity transmission or railways, only one or a few firms can survive, which helps explain natural monopolies. If MES is small, as in hairdressing, many small firms can compete.

Key takeaway: the shape of the long-run average cost curve, especially minimum efficient scale relative to market size, largely decides how many firms an industry can support.

modules.title: Market structures
modules.summary: Perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly compared.

lessons.title: Perfect competition
lessons.summary: Many small price-taking firms selling identical products, and why long-run profit is driven to zero.
lessons.body:
A perfectly competitive market has many buyers and sellers, identical products, full information and free entry and exit. Each firm is a price taker: it can sell as much as it wants at the market price but nothing above it. Its marginal revenue therefore equals the price, MR = P.

Every profit-maximizing firm produces where MR = MC, so a competitive firm produces where P = MC. Profit equals (P − ATC) × Q. In the short run a firm keeps operating as long as price covers average variable cost; below minimum AVC it shuts down. Its short-run supply curve is the MC curve above AVC.

In the long run, positive profits attract entrants, which shifts market supply right and lowers price; losses cause exit. Entry and exit continue until P = minimum ATC, so economic profit is zero. Zero economic profit still means owners earn a normal return on their time and capital.

Key takeaway: perfect competition delivers P = MC (allocative efficiency) and P = minimum ATC (productive efficiency). It is the benchmark against which other market structures are judged.

lessons.title: Monopoly and market power
lessons.summary: A single seller restricts output to raise price, creating profit and deadweight loss.
lessons.body:
A monopoly is the only seller of a product with no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry such as patents, control of a key resource, government licenses or large economies of scale. Facing the whole downward-sloping market demand curve, a monopolist must lower price to sell more, so marginal revenue is below price.

For linear demand P = a − bQ, revenue is aQ − bQ² and MR = a − 2bQ: the MR line has the same intercept and twice the slope. Example: P = 100 − Q and MC = 20. Setting MR = MC gives 100 − 2Q = 20, so Q = 40 and P = 60. A competitive market would produce where P = MC: Q = 80, P = 20. The monopolist halves output, charges three times the price, and creates a deadweight loss of ½ × (80 − 40) × (60 − 20) = 800.

A useful summary is the Lerner index, L = (P − MC) ÷ P = 1 ÷ |Ed|: market power is greater when demand is less elastic. Governments respond with competition law, regulation of natural monopolies (for example price caps) or by lowering entry barriers.

Key takeaway: a monopolist sets MR = MC, then charges the highest price demand allows at that quantity. The result is higher prices, lower output and deadweight loss compared with competition.

lessons.title: Monopolistic competition
lessons.summary: Many firms with differentiated products: some pricing power in the short run, zero profit in the long run.
lessons.body:
Monopolistic competition combines features of competition and monopoly. There are many firms and free entry, but each sells a differentiated product: restaurants, clothing brands, hair salons and mobile apps are typical examples. Differentiation gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve and some control over its price.

In the short run a firm behaves like a small monopolist, producing where MR = MC and possibly earning profit. That profit attracts new entrants offering similar products, which takes customers away and shifts each firm's demand curve left. In long-run equilibrium the demand curve is tangent to the ATC curve, so P = ATC and economic profit is zero.

Unlike perfect competition, price is above marginal cost and firms produce below the output that minimizes ATC, which is called excess capacity. The benefit to consumers is variety. Firms spend heavily on advertising and branding because stronger differentiation makes demand less elastic and protects margins.

Key takeaway: differentiation buys short-run pricing power, but free entry erodes profit to zero in the long run. Expect P > MC, excess capacity and strong spending on brands.

lessons.title: Oligopoly and game theory
lessons.summary: When a few firms dominate, each must anticipate rivals’ moves; game theory models these strategic choices.
lessons.body:
An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms, such as mobile networks, airlines or cement producers. Because each firm's profit depends on what rivals do, decisions are strategic, and game theory is the natural tool.

The classic model is the prisoner's dilemma. Two firms each choose a high or low price. If both price high, each earns 10; if both price low, each earns 6; if one undercuts, it earns 14 while the other earns 2. Whatever the rival does, pricing low pays more (14 > 10 and 6 > 2), so low is a dominant strategy and the Nash equilibrium is (low, low), even though both would be better off at (high, high). A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where no player can gain by changing only their own choice.

This explains why cartels are unstable: each member is tempted to cheat on the agreed output. Repeated interaction can sustain cooperation through strategies such as tit-for-tat, which is why competition authorities watch for tacit collusion. Other oligopoly models include Cournot (firms choose quantities) and Bertrand (firms choose prices; with identical products, price falls to marginal cost even with two firms).

Key takeaway: in oligopoly, the best decision depends on rivals' decisions. Look for dominant strategies and Nash equilibria, and expect cooperation to be fragile unless the game is repeated.

scarcity-opportunity-cost.title: Tanqislik va muqobil xarajat
scarcity-opportunity-cost.summary: Har bir tanlovda nimadandir voz kechiladi; muqobil xarajat — voz kechilgan eng yaxshi muqobilning qiymati.
scarcity-opportunity-cost.body:
Iqtisodiyot tanqislikdan boshlanadi: ehtiyojlar cheksiz, ammo vaqt, pul va resurslar cheklangan. Shu sababli har bir tanlovning muqobil xarajati bor — bu siz voz kechgan keyingi eng yaxshi muqobilning qiymati. U barcha muqobillarning yig‘indisi emas, faqat eng yaxshisidir.

Misol: talaba shanba kuni 150 000 so‘m to‘lanadigan smenada ishlashi yoki imtihonga tayyorlanishi mumkin. Agar u o‘qishni tanlasa, o‘qishning muqobil xarajati yo‘qotilgan 150 000 so‘m ish haqi hamda smenadan oladigan boshqa foydalaridir. Ishlab chiqarish imkoniyatlari chegarasi (IICh) shu g‘oyani butun iqtisodiyot uchun tasvirlaydi: egri chiziq bo‘ylab bir tovarni ko‘proq ishlab chiqarish boshqasini kamroq ishlab chiqarishni anglatadi, egri chiziq qiyaligi esa muqobil xarajatdir.

Asosiy xulosa: iqtisodiyotda xarajat faqat to‘langan pul bilan emas, balki voz kechilgan narsa bilan o‘lchanadi. Oqilona qaror variantning foydasini uning to‘liq muqobil xarajati bilan solishtiradi.

demand-curve.title: Talab va talab qonuni
demand-curve.summary: Nima uchun narx oshganda talab miqdori kamayadi hamda talab egri chizig‘i bo‘ylab harakat va egri chiziqning siljishi o‘rtasidagi farq.
demand-curve.body:
Talab qonuniga ko‘ra, boshqa sharoitlar o‘zgarmagan holda, narx oshsa talab miqdori kamayadi. Talab egri chizig‘ida vertikal o‘qda narx, gorizontal o‘qda miqdor ko‘rsatiladi va u pastga qarab qiyalanadi. Chiziqli misol: Qd = 100 − 2P. P = 10 bo‘lganda xaridorlar 80 birlik, P = 20 bo‘lganda 60 birlik xohlaydi.

Ikki xil o‘zgarishni ajratish juda muhim. Tovarning o‘z narxi o‘zgarsa, egri chiziq bo‘ylab harakat yuz beradi (talab miqdorining o‘zgarishi). Boshqa har qanday omil o‘zgarsa, butun egri chiziq siljiydi (talabning o‘zgarishi). Asosiy omillar: daromad (normal tovarlarga talab daromad bilan oshadi, past sifatli tovarlarga kamayadi), o‘rinbosar va to‘ldiruvchi tovarlar narxlari, didlar, kelajakdagi narxlar bo‘yicha kutishlar va xaridorlar soni.

Asosiy xulosa: narx sizni talab egri chizig‘i bo‘ylab harakatlantiradi; daromad, bog‘liq tovarlar narxi, didlar, kutishlar va aholi soni esa uni siljitadi. Bu ikkisini chalkashtirish bozor tahlilidagi eng keng tarqalgan xatodir.

supply-equilibrium.title: Taklif va bozor muvozanati
supply-equilibrium.summary: Taklif egri chizig‘i ishlab chiqaruvchilarning xarajatlaridan qanday tuziladi va talab bilan taklif qayerda kesishadi.
supply-equilibrium.body:
Taklif qonuniga ko‘ra, narx oshsa firmalar sotishga tayyor bo‘lgan miqdor ortadi, chunki yuqori narx qo‘shimcha birliklarni ishlab chiqarishning yuqoriroq xarajatini qoplaydi. Xomashyo narxi, texnologiya, soliqlar, sotuvchilar soni yoki kutishlar o‘zgarsa, taklif siljiydi.

Muvozanat — talab miqdori taklif miqdoriga teng bo‘lgan narx. Qd = 100 − 2P va Qs = −20 + 4P bo‘lsa, ularni tenglashtiramiz: 100 − 2P = −20 + 4P, demak 6P = 120 va P* = 20. Unda Q* = 100 − 40 = 60 birlik. 20 dan yuqori narxda ortiqcha taklif yuzaga kelib narxni tushiradi; 20 dan pastda esa taqchillik narxni ko‘taradi.

Qiyosiy statika — zarbadan oldingi va keyingi muvozanatlarni solishtirish. Qurg‘oqchilik xarajatlarni oshirsa, taklif chapga siljiydi: narx oshadi, miqdor kamayadi. Normal tovar uchun daromad oshsa, talab o‘ngga siljiydi: narx ham, miqdor ham oshadi. Ikkala egri chiziq bir vaqtda siljisa, natijalardan biri noaniq bo‘lib, har bir siljish kattaligiga bog‘liq bo‘ladi.

Asosiy xulosa: muvozanat narxini topish uchun Qd = Qs tenglamasini yeching, so‘ng miqdorni topish uchun narxni qayta qo‘ying. Zarbani bashorat qilish uchun qaysi egri chiziq, qaysi yo‘nalishda siljishini aniqlang va yangi kesishish nuqtasini o‘qing.

elasticity.title: Talabning narx bo‘yicha elastikligi
elasticity.summary: Xaridorlarning narx o‘zgarishiga qanchalik kuchli javob berishini o‘lchash va uning tushumga ta’siri.
elasticity.body:
Talabning narx bo‘yicha elastikligi talab miqdorining narxga qanchalik sezgir ekanini o‘lchaydi: Ed = (miqdorning % o‘zgarishi) ÷ (narxning % o‘zgarishi). O‘rta nuqta usuli yo‘nalishga qarab turli javob olishning oldini oladi: %ΔQ = ΔQ ÷ o‘rtacha Q.

Misol: qahvaxona qahva narxini 10 000 so‘mdan 12 000 so‘mga oshirganda kunlik sotuv 220 stakandan 180 stakanga tushdi. %ΔQ = −40 ÷ 200 = −20%, %ΔP = 2 000 ÷ 11 000 ≈ 18,2%, demak |Ed| ≈ 1,1. Xaridorlar kuchli javob bersa talab elastik (|Ed| > 1), deyarli javob bermasa noelastik (|Ed| < 1), aynan 1 ga teng bo‘lsa birlik elastikdir.

Elastiklik umumiy tushum (P × Q) bilan nima bo‘lishini belgilaydi. Talab elastik bo‘lsa, narxni oshirish tushumni kamaytiradi; noelastik bo‘lsa, narxni oshirish tushumni ko‘paytiradi. Yaqin o‘rinbosarlar mavjud bo‘lsa, tovar byudjetning katta qismini tashkil etsa, u hashamatli tovar bo‘lsa va uzoq muddatda talab elastikroq bo‘ladi.

Asosiy xulosa: narxni o‘zgartirishdan oldin elastiklikni baholang. Noelastik talabda narx oshishi tushumni ko‘paytiradi, elastik talabda esa kamaytiradi.

utility-marginal-utility.title: Naflilik va kamayuvchi chekli naflilik
utility-marginal-utility.summary: Iste’molchilar tovarning har bir qo‘shimcha birligidan kamroq qo‘shimcha qoniqish oladi.
utility-marginal-utility.body:
Naflilik — tovarlar to‘plami beradigan qoniqishni tartiblash usuli. Qarorlar uchun chekli naflilik (MU) muhim: bir birlik ko‘proq tovardan olinadigan qo‘shimcha naflilik. Ko‘pchilik tovarlar uchun chekli naflilik kamayib boradi: issiq kunda birinchi stakan suv juda qimmatli, beshinchisi esa ancha kamroq.

Iste’molchi har bir tovarga sarflangan oxirgi so‘m bir xil qo‘shimcha qoniqish berganda oqilona sarflaydi. Bu teng chekli naflilik tamoyili: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. Agar MUx ÷ Px kattaroq bo‘lsa, xarajatni y dan x ga o‘tkazish umumiy naflilikni oshiradi, kamayuvchi chekli naflilik esa nisbatlar oxir-oqibat tenglashishini kafolatlaydi.

Misol: non 4 000 so‘m turadi va keyingi non MU = 20 beradi (har 1 000 so‘mga 5); choy 10 000 so‘m turadi va MU = 30 beradi (har 1 000 so‘mga 3). Iste’molchi nisbatlar tenglashguncha ko‘proq non va kamroq choy sotib olishi kerak.

Asosiy xulosa: qarorlar chekli miqdorda qabul qilinadi. Kamayuvchi chekli naflilik talab egri chizig‘i pastga qiyalanishining xulq-atvor sababidir.

budget-constraint.title: Byudjet cheklovi va optimal tanlov
budget-constraint.summary: Byudjet chizig‘i iste’molchi nimaga qurbi yetishini ko‘rsatadi; eng yaxshi to‘plam u eng yuqori befarqlik egri chizig‘iga tegib o‘tgan nuqtadir.
budget-constraint.body:
Byudjet cheklovi iste’molchi sotib olishga qurbi yetadigan barcha to‘plamlarni ko‘rsatadi: Px·X + Py·Y = I, bu yerda I — daromad. X gorizontal o‘qda bo‘lganda byudjet chizig‘ining qiyaligi −Px ÷ Py ga teng, ya’ni bir tovarning boshqasiga almashinadigan bozor nisbati. Daromad oshsa, chiziq parallel ravishda tashqariga siljiydi; X narxi oshsa, chiziq X o‘qi bo‘ylab ichkariga buriladi.

Afzalliklar befarqlik egri chiziqlari bilan tasvirlanadi — har biri iste’molchi uchun bir xil darajada yoqimli to‘plamlarni birlashtiradi. Ularning qiyaligi chekli almashtirish normasi (MRS = MUx ÷ MUy), ya’ni iste’molchi almashishga tayyor bo‘lgan nisbat. Optimal nuqta MRS = Px ÷ Py bo‘lgan urinish nuqtasidir: almashishga tayyorlik bozor narxlari nisbatiga teng.

Misol: daromad 100 000 so‘m, Px = 10 000 va Py = 5 000 bo‘lsa, iste’molchi ko‘pi bilan 10 birlik X yoki 20 birlik Y sotib oladi. X narxining pasayishi X ni nisbatan arzonlashtiradi (almashtirish samarasi) va real xarid qobiliyatini oshiradi (daromad samarasi).

Asosiy xulosa: optimal tanlov qurbi yetadigan narsa (byudjet chizig‘i) va afzal ko‘riladigan narsani (befarqlik egri chiziqlari) birlashtiradi. Har bir narx o‘zgarishining almashtirish samarasi va daromad samarasi bor.

consumer-producer-surplus.title: Iste’molchi ortiqcha nafi, ishlab chiqaruvchi ortiqcha nafi va sof yo‘qotish
consumer-producer-surplus.summary: Savdodan olinadigan foyda hamda soliqlar va narx nazorati keltiradigan yo‘qotishlarni o‘lchash.
consumer-producer-surplus.body:
Iste’molchi ortiqcha nafi — xaridorlar to‘lashga tayyor bo‘lgan summa bilan amalda to‘lagan summa o‘rtasidagi farq; grafikda u talab egri chizig‘idan pastda va narxdan yuqorida joylashgan maydon. Ishlab chiqaruvchi ortiqcha nafi — sotuvchilar oladigan narx bilan ular rozi bo‘ladigan eng past narx o‘rtasidagi farq; bu taklif egri chizig‘idan yuqori va narxdan pastdagi maydon. Ularning yig‘indisi umumiy ortiqcha naf, ya’ni bozor yaratadigan iqtisodiy qiymatdir.

Misol: Qd = 100 − 2P va Qs = −20 + 4P bo‘lsa, muvozanat P* = 20, Q* = 60. Talab P = 50 da nolga teng, demak iste’molchi ortiqcha nafi = ½ × 60 × (50 − 20) = 900. Taklif P = 5 dan boshlanadi, demak ishlab chiqaruvchi ortiqcha nafi = ½ × 60 × (20 − 5) = 450. Umumiy ortiqcha naf 1 350 ga teng.

Raqobatli muvozanat umumiy ortiqcha nafni maksimallashtiradi. Soliqlar, narxning yuqori va quyi chegaralari miqdorni Q* dan uzoqlashtiradi, endi amalga oshmaydigan bitimlar qiymati esa sof yo‘qotish bo‘lib, egri chiziqlar orasidagi uchburchak bilan ifodalanadi. Masalan, muvozanatdan past ijara narxi chegarasi ba’zi ijarachilar yutsa-da, taqchillik va sof yo‘qotishni keltirib chiqaradi.

Asosiy xulosa: ortiqcha naf bozordan kim yutishini o‘lchaydi. Miqdorni muvozanatdan uzoqlashtiradigan aralashuvlar jamiyat uchun sof yo‘qotish keltiradi.

production-function.title: Ishlab chiqarish funksiyasi va kamayuvchi samaradorlik
production-function.summary: Mahsulot resurslarga bog‘liq va bitta resursni ko‘paytirish oxir-oqibat kamroq qo‘shimcha mahsulot beradi.
production-function.body:
Ishlab chiqarish funksiyasi firma berilgan resurslardan ishlab chiqarishi mumkin bo‘lgan eng ko‘p mahsulotni ko‘rsatadi va ko‘pincha mehnat hamda kapital uchun Q = f(L, K) ko‘rinishida yoziladi. Qisqa muddatda kamida bitta resurs, odatda kapital, o‘zgarmas bo‘ladi. Mehnatning chekli mahsuloti (MPL) — yana bitta ishchidan olinadigan qo‘shimcha mahsulot.

Kamayuvchi chekli samaradorlik qonuniga ko‘ra, o‘zgarmas kapitalga ishchilarni qo‘shib borsangiz, MPL oxir-oqibat kamayadi. Ikkita pechli novvoyxonada ikkinchi novvoy qo‘shilganda mahsulot 100 dan 180 nonga oshishi, uchinchisi qo‘shilganda esa atigi 220 ga yetishi mumkin, chunki novvoylar pech bo‘shashini kuta boshlaydi.

Keng tarqalgan funksiya shakli — Kobb-Duglas: Q = A·L^a·K^b. Agar a + b = 1 bo‘lsa, miqyosdan doimiy samara bor (barcha resurslarni ikki baravar oshirish mahsulotni ikki baravar oshiradi); a + b > 1 — o‘suvchi, a + b < 1 — kamayuvchi samara. Miqyos samarasi barcha resurslar o‘zgara oladigan uzoq muddatni, kamayuvchi samaradorlik esa qisqa muddatni tavsiflaydi.

Asosiy xulosa: kamayuvchi chekli samaradorlik — bitta resurs o‘zgarmas bo‘lgan qisqa muddatli tushuncha. Miqyos samarasi — barcha resurslarni birga oshirish haqidagi uzoq muddatli tushuncha.

short-run-costs.title: Doimiy, o‘zgaruvchan, chekli va o‘rtacha xarajatlar
short-run-costs.summary: Har bir firma qancha ishlab chiqarishni hal qilishda foydalanadigan xarajat egri chiziqlari.
short-run-costs.body:
Umumiy xarajat ishlab chiqarish hajmiga bog‘liq bo‘lmagan doimiy xarajat (FC), masalan ijara, va hajmga bog‘liq o‘zgaruvchan xarajatga (VC), masalan un va soatbay ish haqiga bo‘linadi: TC = FC + VC. Ularni mahsulot miqdoriga bo‘lsak, o‘rtacha doimiy, o‘rtacha o‘zgaruvchan va o‘rtacha umumiy xarajat hosil bo‘ladi: ATC = TC ÷ Q.

Chekli xarajat — yana bir birlik ishlab chiqarishning qo‘shimcha xarajati: MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ yoki dTC/dQ hosilasi. Kamayuvchi samaradorlik tufayli MC oxir-oqibat oshadi va bu ATC egri chizig‘ini U shakliga keltiradi. MC har doim ATC va AVC ni ularning eng past nuqtasida kesib o‘tadi: chekli birlik o‘rtachadan arzon bo‘lsa, o‘rtachani pasaytiradi, qimmat bo‘lsa — oshiradi.

Misol: TC = 500 + 10Q + Q². Doimiy xarajat 500 ga, MC = 10 + 2Q ga teng. ATC = 500/Q + 10 + Q eng kichik qiymatga MC = ATC bo‘lganda erishadi: 10 + 2Q = 500/Q + 10 + Q, demak Q² = 500 va Q ≈ 22,4 birlik.

Asosiy xulosa: chekli xarajat ishlab chiqarish qarorlarini belgilaydi; o‘rtacha xarajat firma foyda ko‘rayotganini ko‘rsatadi. MC ATC ni uning eng past nuqtasida kesib o‘tadi.

economies-of-scale.title: Uzoq muddatli xarajatlar va miqyos tejamkorligi
economies-of-scale.summary: Nima uchun ba’zi firmalar o‘sganda o‘rtacha xarajat kamayadi va ular haddan tashqari kattalashganda nima uchun oshadi.
economies-of-scale.body:
Uzoq muddatda firma korxona hajmini tanlay oladi, shuning uchun barcha xarajatlar o‘zgaruvchan bo‘ladi. Uzoq muddatli o‘rtacha xarajat (LRAC) egri chizig‘i firma har bir hajm uchun eng yaxshi korxonani tanlaganda erishiladigan eng past o‘rtacha xarajatni ko‘rsatadi.

Miqyos tejamkorligi ishlab chiqarish o‘sishi bilan LRAC kamayganda yuzaga keladi. Uning manbalari: ishchilarning ixtisoslashuvi, dasturiy ta’minot yoki zavod kabi yirik doimiy investitsiyalarni ko‘proq birlikka taqsimlash va ulgurji xarid chegirmalari. Miqyosning salbiy samarasi muvofiqlashtirish qiyinlashib, boshqaruv bo‘g‘inlari ko‘paygani sababli LRAC oshganda yuz beradi. Ular orasida ko‘pincha doimiy samarali tekis oraliq bo‘ladi.

Minimal samarali miqyos (MES) — LRAC eng past darajaga yetadigan eng kichik hajm. Agar MES bozor talabiga nisbatan katta bo‘lsa (elektr uzatish yoki temir yo‘llarda bo‘lgani kabi), faqat bitta yoki bir nechta firma yashab qola oladi, bu tabiiy monopoliyalarni tushuntiradi. MES kichik bo‘lsa (sartaroshlikda bo‘lgani kabi), ko‘plab kichik firmalar raqobatlasha oladi.

Asosiy xulosa: uzoq muddatli o‘rtacha xarajat egri chizig‘ining shakli, ayniqsa bozor hajmiga nisbatan minimal samarali miqyos, tarmoq nechta firmani ko‘tara olishini asosan belgilaydi.

perfect-competition.title: Mukammal raqobat
perfect-competition.summary: Bir xil mahsulot sotadigan, narxni qabul qiluvchi ko‘plab kichik firmalar va nima uchun uzoq muddatli foyda nolga tushadi.
perfect-competition.body:
Mukammal raqobatli bozorda ko‘plab xaridor va sotuvchilar, bir xil mahsulotlar, to‘liq axborot hamda erkin kirish va chiqish mavjud. Har bir firma narxni qabul qiluvchidir: u bozor narxida xohlagancha sota oladi, lekin undan yuqori narxda hech narsa sotolmaydi. Shuning uchun uning chekli daromadi narxga teng: MR = P.

Foydani maksimallashtiruvchi har bir firma MR = MC bo‘lgan nuqtada ishlab chiqaradi, demak raqobatli firma P = MC nuqtasida ishlab chiqaradi. Foyda (P − ATC) × Q ga teng. Qisqa muddatda firma narx o‘rtacha o‘zgaruvchan xarajatni qoplagunga qadar ishlashda davom etadi; minimal AVC dan pastda u faoliyatni to‘xtatadi. Uning qisqa muddatli taklif egri chizig‘i — AVC dan yuqoridagi MC egri chizig‘i.

Uzoq muddatda ijobiy foyda yangi firmalarni jalb qiladi, bu bozor taklifini o‘ngga siljitib, narxni pasaytiradi; zararlar esa firmalarning chiqishiga sabab bo‘ladi. Kirish va chiqish P = minimal ATC bo‘lgunga qadar davom etadi, shuning uchun iqtisodiy foyda nolga teng. Nol iqtisodiy foyda baribir egalar o‘z vaqti va kapitali uchun normal daromad olishini bildiradi.

Asosiy xulosa: mukammal raqobat P = MC (taqsimot samaradorligi) va P = minimal ATC (ishlab chiqarish samaradorligi) natijasini beradi. U boshqa bozor tuzilmalarini baholashda andoza hisoblanadi.

monopoly.title: Monopoliya va bozor hokimiyati
monopoly.summary: Yagona sotuvchi narxni oshirish uchun ishlab chiqarishni cheklaydi, bu esa foyda va sof yo‘qotishni keltirib chiqaradi.
monopoly.body:
Monopoliya — yaqin o‘rinbosari bo‘lmagan mahsulotning yagona sotuvchisi bo‘lib, u patentlar, asosiy resurs ustidan nazorat, davlat litsenziyalari yoki katta miqyos tejamkorligi kabi kirish to‘siqlari bilan himoyalangan. Pastga qiyalangan butun bozor talabiga duch kelgan monopolist ko‘proq sotish uchun narxni tushirishi kerak, shuning uchun chekli daromad narxdan past bo‘ladi.

Chiziqli talab P = a − bQ uchun tushum aQ − bQ², MR = a − 2bQ: MR chizig‘i xuddi shu kesishma nuqtasiga va ikki baravar katta qiyalikka ega. Misol: P = 100 − Q va MC = 20. MR = MC tenglamasi 100 − 2Q = 20 ni beradi, demak Q = 40 va P = 60. Raqobatli bozor P = MC nuqtasida ishlab chiqarar edi: Q = 80, P = 20. Monopolist ishlab chiqarishni ikki baravar qisqartiradi, uch baravar yuqori narx qo‘yadi va ½ × (80 − 40) × (60 − 20) = 800 miqdorida sof yo‘qotish yaratadi.

Foydali umumlashma — Lerner indeksi: L = (P − MC) ÷ P = 1 ÷ |Ed|. Talab qanchalik kam elastik bo‘lsa, bozor hokimiyati shunchalik kuchli. Davlatlar bunga raqobat to‘g‘risidagi qonunlar, tabiiy monopoliyalarni tartibga solish (masalan, narx chegaralari) yoki kirish to‘siqlarini pasaytirish orqali javob beradi.

Asosiy xulosa: monopolist MR = MC ni o‘rnatadi, so‘ng shu miqdorda talab imkon beradigan eng yuqori narxni qo‘yadi. Natijada raqobatga nisbatan narxlar yuqori, ishlab chiqarish past bo‘ladi va sof yo‘qotish paydo bo‘ladi.

monopolistic-competition.title: Monopolistik raqobat
monopolistic-competition.summary: Farqlangan mahsulotlarga ega ko‘plab firmalar: qisqa muddatda biroz narx hokimiyati, uzoq muddatda nol foyda.
monopolistic-competition.body:
Monopolistik raqobat raqobat va monopoliya xususiyatlarini birlashtiradi. Firmalar ko‘p va kirish erkin, lekin har biri farqlangan mahsulot sotadi: restoranlar, kiyim brendlari, sartaroshxonalar va mobil ilovalar odatiy misollardir. Farqlanish har bir firmaga pastga qiyalangan talab egri chizig‘i va narxi ustidan ma’lum nazorat beradi.

Qisqa muddatda firma kichik monopolist kabi harakat qiladi: MR = MC nuqtasida ishlab chiqaradi va foyda olishi mumkin. Bu foyda o‘xshash mahsulot taklif qiluvchi yangi firmalarni jalb qiladi, ular mijozlarni olib ketadi va har bir firmaning talab egri chizig‘ini chapga siljitadi. Uzoq muddatli muvozanatda talab egri chizig‘i ATC egri chizig‘iga urinadi, shuning uchun P = ATC va iqtisodiy foyda nolga teng.

Mukammal raqobatdan farqli o‘laroq, narx chekli xarajatdan yuqori va firmalar ATC ni minimallashtiradigan hajmdan kamroq ishlab chiqaradi — bu ortiqcha quvvat deyiladi. Iste’molchilar uchun foyda — xilma-xillik. Firmalar reklama va brendingga ko‘p sarflaydi, chunki kuchliroq farqlanish talabni kamroq elastik qiladi va ustamani himoya qiladi.

Asosiy xulosa: farqlanish qisqa muddatli narx hokimiyatini beradi, lekin erkin kirish uzoq muddatda foydani nolga tushiradi. P > MC, ortiqcha quvvat va brendlarga katta xarajatlarni kuting.

oligopoly-game-theory.title: Oligopoliya va o‘yinlar nazariyasi
oligopoly-game-theory.summary: Bozorda bir nechta firma hukmron bo‘lsa, har biri raqiblarning harakatini oldindan ko‘rishi kerak; o‘yinlar nazariyasi bu strategik tanlovlarni modellashtiradi.
oligopoly-game-theory.body:
Oligopoliya — mobil aloqa operatorlari, aviakompaniyalar yoki sement ishlab chiqaruvchilar kabi bir nechta yirik firma hukmron bo‘lgan bozor. Har bir firmaning foydasi raqiblar nima qilishiga bog‘liq bo‘lgani uchun qarorlar strategik xususiyatga ega va o‘yinlar nazariyasi buning uchun tabiiy vositadir.

Klassik model — mahbus dilemmasi. Ikki firma yuqori yoki past narxni tanlaydi. Ikkalasi yuqori narx qo‘ysa, har biri 10 dan oladi; ikkalasi past narx qo‘ysa, har biri 6 dan; biri narxni tushirsa, u 14, ikkinchisi esa 2 oladi. Raqib nima qilishidan qat’i nazar, past narx ko‘proq foyda beradi (14 > 10 va 6 > 2), demak past narx ustun strategiya va Nesh muvozanati (past, past) bo‘ladi, garchi ikkalasi uchun (yuqori, yuqori) yaxshiroq bo‘lsa ham. Nesh muvozanati — hech bir o‘yinchi faqat o‘z tanlovini o‘zgartirib yutolmaydigan strategiyalar to‘plami.

Bu kartellarning nima uchun beqarorligini tushuntiradi: har bir a’zo kelishilgan hajmni buzish vasvasasiga tushadi. Takroriy o‘zaro ta’sir "qasosga qasos" kabi strategiyalar orqali hamkorlikni saqlab qolishi mumkin, shu sababli raqobat organlari yashirin til biriktirishni kuzatadi. Boshqa oligopoliya modellari: Kurno (firmalar miqdorni tanlaydi) va Bertran (firmalar narxni tanlaydi; bir xil mahsulotlarda hatto ikki firma bo‘lsa ham narx chekli xarajatgacha tushadi).

Asosiy xulosa: oligopoliyada eng yaxshi qaror raqiblarning qarorlariga bog‘liq. Ustun strategiyalar va Nesh muvozanatini izlang hamda o‘yin takrorlanmasa, hamkorlik mo‘rt bo‘lishini kuting.

topics.title: Macroeconomics & Monetary Policy
topics.description: Measure the whole economy with GDP, inflation and unemployment, explain booms and recessions with aggregate demand and supply, and see how central banks use interest rates and money to stabilize prices and output.

modules.title: Measuring the economy
modules.summary: GDP, inflation and unemployment: the three numbers every macroeconomic debate begins with.

lessons.title: Gross domestic product
lessons.summary: GDP measures the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period.
lessons.body:
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period. "Final" means intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting: the flour a bakery buys is counted inside the price of the bread, not separately.

The expenditure approach adds up who buys the output: GDP = C + I + G + NX, where C is household consumption, I is business investment (including new housing and inventories), G is government purchases, and NX is exports minus imports. Transfers such as pensions are not in G because they do not buy new output. The same total can be reached by summing incomes (wages, profits, rent) or value added at each production stage.

Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses constant base-year prices, so it changes only when quantities change. The GDP deflator is (nominal ÷ real) × 100. Example: if nominal GDP rises 14% and the deflator rises 9%, real growth is roughly 14% − 9% = 5%. GDP per capita divides by population and is a rough guide to living standards, but it ignores leisure, inequality, informal work and environmental damage.

Key takeaway: GDP = C + I + G + NX. Use real GDP to compare output over time, and remember what GDP leaves out.

lessons.title: Inflation and price indexes
lessons.summary: How the consumer price index measures the cost of living and why inflation matters.
lessons.body:
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. It is usually measured with the consumer price index (CPI), which prices a fixed basket of goods and services a typical household buys. CPI in year t = (cost of basket in year t ÷ cost in base year) × 100, and the inflation rate is the percentage change in CPI: (CPI now − CPI a year ago) ÷ CPI a year ago.

Example: a basket costs 4,000,000 UZS in the base year and 4,400,000 UZS a year later. CPI moves from 100 to 110, so inflation is 10%. A worker whose wage rose 7% has suffered a real wage cut of about 3%. The Fisher relation links rates in the same way: real interest rate ≈ nominal interest rate − expected inflation.

CPI tends to overstate true cost-of-living increases because of substitution bias (households switch to cheaper goods), new products and quality improvements. Core inflation excludes volatile food and energy prices to reveal the underlying trend. Inflation is costly when it is high or unpredictable: it redistributes wealth from savers to borrowers, distorts price signals and raises uncertainty. Deflation, a falling price level, is also dangerous because it raises the real burden of debt.

Key takeaway: inflation = percentage change in a price index. Always convert nominal values to real ones by subtracting inflation.

lessons.title: Unemployment and the labor market
lessons.summary: How unemployment is measured and the difference between frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment.
lessons.body:
The labor force is everyone who is working or actively looking for work. The unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labor force × 100. People who have stopped searching (discouraged workers) are not counted in the labor force, so the official rate can understate labor market weakness. The labor force participation rate = labor force ÷ working-age population.

Economists distinguish three types of unemployment. Frictional unemployment comes from the time it takes to match workers and jobs, such as a graduate searching for a first position. Structural unemployment arises when workers' skills or locations do not match available jobs, for example after automation or the decline of an industry. Cyclical unemployment rises in recessions when demand falls. The natural rate of unemployment is frictional plus structural; when actual unemployment equals the natural rate, the economy is at potential output.

Okun's law summarizes the link between output and jobs: in many economies, each 1 percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate corresponds to output roughly 2% below potential. Example: with 1,000 people working and 80 searching, the labor force is 1,080 and the unemployment rate is 80 ÷ 1,080 ≈ 7.4%.

Key takeaway: unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labor force. Only cyclical unemployment is the target of demand-side stabilization policy; structural unemployment needs training and labor-market reforms.

modules.title: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
modules.summary: A single framework for growth, recessions and inflation, and the role of fiscal policy.

lessons.title: Aggregate demand and the multiplier
lessons.summary: Total spending in the economy, what shifts it, and why an initial change in spending gets amplified.
lessons.body:
Aggregate demand (AD) is total planned spending on domestic output at each price level: AD = C + I + G + NX. The AD curve slopes downward because a lower price level raises the real value of money and wealth, lowers interest rates and makes exports cheaper. AD shifts when consumer or business confidence changes, when government spending or taxes change, when the central bank changes interest rates, or when foreign demand changes.

An initial change in spending is amplified because one person's spending is another's income. If households spend a fraction MPC (marginal propensity to consume) of each extra som, the spending multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). With MPC = 0.8 the multiplier is 5: a 10 trillion UZS rise in government investment could raise GDP by up to 50 trillion UZS in a simple closed economy. In practice multipliers are much smaller because part of extra income is taxed, saved or spent on imports, and because interest rates may rise.

Key takeaway: AD = C + I + G + NX, and spending changes ripple through the economy via the multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). Real-world multipliers are reduced by taxes, imports and saving.

lessons.title: Short-run and long-run aggregate supply
lessons.summary: Why output can deviate from potential in the short run but returns to it in the long run.
lessons.body:
Aggregate supply (AS) shows how much output firms produce at each price level. In the long run, output is set by real resources (labor, capital, technology and institutions), not by the price level, so the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve is vertical at potential output Y*. Growth in LRAS is what raises living standards over decades.

In the short run, many wages and prices are sticky: contracts and menus are not rewritten every week. When the price level rises unexpectedly, firms' selling prices rise faster than their costs, so they produce more. The short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve therefore slopes upward. SRAS shifts left when input costs rise, for example after an oil price shock or a jump in wages, and right when costs fall or productivity improves.

The intersection of AD and SRAS gives short-run output and the price level. If output is below Y*, there is a recessionary gap with high unemployment; if above Y*, an inflationary gap. Over time, wages and prices adjust and SRAS shifts until the economy returns to Y*. A supply shock is especially difficult because it raises prices and lowers output at the same time, which is called stagflation.

Key takeaway: in the long run output is fixed at potential and only the price level adjusts; in the short run sticky prices let demand and cost shocks move output.

lessons.title: Fiscal policy and public debt
lessons.summary: How government spending and taxation stabilize demand, and the limits set by deficits and debt.
lessons.body:
Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxes to influence the economy. Expansionary fiscal policy (higher spending or lower taxes) shifts AD right to close a recessionary gap; contractionary policy (lower spending or higher taxes) shifts AD left to cool an overheating economy. Automatic stabilizers such as unemployment benefits and progressive income taxes work without new legislation: they rise or fall with the business cycle and cushion swings in income.

A budget deficit occurs when spending exceeds revenue in a year; public debt is the accumulated stock of past deficits. What matters for sustainability is the debt-to-GDP ratio. It stays stable when the primary balance (the budget balance excluding interest payments) is large enough relative to the gap between the interest rate on debt and the growth rate of GDP. If interest rates are well above growth, a country must run primary surpluses just to keep the ratio steady.

Fiscal policy has limits. Decisions and spending take time (implementation lags), extra government borrowing can raise interest rates and crowd out private investment, and large debts reduce space to respond to the next crisis. In small open economies, part of any stimulus leaks abroad through imports.

Key takeaway: fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand through spending and taxes. Watch the debt-to-GDP ratio and the gap between interest rates and growth to judge whether deficits are sustainable.

modules.title: Money and banking
modules.summary: What money is, how banks create it, and how the money supply relates to prices.

lessons.title: What money is and does
lessons.summary: Money as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value, and how the money supply is measured.
lessons.body:
Money is any asset that is widely accepted in payment. It performs three functions. As a medium of exchange it removes the need for a double coincidence of wants that barter requires. As a unit of account it gives a common measure for prices, contracts and accounts. As a store of value it lets people move purchasing power into the future, although inflation erodes this function.

Modern money is fiat money: it has value because the state declares it legal tender and people trust it, not because it is backed by gold. Most money is not cash but bank deposits. Central banks measure the money supply with aggregates: M0 or the monetary base (cash plus banks' reserves at the central bank), M1 (cash in circulation plus demand deposits), and M2 (M1 plus savings and time deposits). In economies where many deposits are in foreign currency, analysts also track dollarization, the share of deposits and loans in dollars, because it weakens the central bank's control.

Key takeaway: money is defined by what it does, not what it is made of. Most of the money supply consists of bank deposits rather than physical cash.

lessons.title: How banks create money
lessons.summary: Fractional-reserve banking, the money multiplier and why bank lending expands the money supply.
lessons.body:
Commercial banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest. When a bank makes a loan, it credits the borrower's account with a new deposit, and that deposit is new money. When the borrower spends it, the money lands in another bank, which can lend part of it again.

The simple money multiplier shows the maximum expansion: money multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio. With a 10% reserve requirement, an extra 1 billion UZS of reserves can support up to 10 billion UZS of deposits. A bank's balance sheet shows the logic: assets (reserves, loans, securities) = liabilities (deposits, borrowing) + equity capital.

In reality the multiplier is not mechanical. Banks lend when they find creditworthy borrowers and when lending is profitable, and they are constrained more by capital requirements and risk than by reserves. Households also hold some cash, which reduces the multiplier. That is why modern central banks steer the price of money (the interest rate) rather than trying to control the quantity of reserves directly.

Key takeaway: bank loans create deposits, and deposits are money. The multiplier 1 ÷ reserve ratio is an upper bound, not a precise forecast.

lessons.title: Money, prices and the quantity theory
lessons.summary: The equation of exchange links money growth to inflation over the long run.
lessons.body:
The equation of exchange is an identity: M × V = P × Y, where M is the money supply, V is velocity (how many times a unit of money is spent per year), P is the price level and Y is real output. P × Y is nominal GDP.

The quantity theory adds two assumptions: velocity is fairly stable, and real output is determined by real factors in the long run. In growth rates the identity becomes: money growth + velocity growth ≈ inflation + real GDP growth. If V is stable, inflation ≈ money growth − real output growth. Example: if the money supply grows 20% a year and real GDP grows 5%, long-run inflation will be around 15%.

The evidence strongly supports this over long periods and across countries: every episode of very high inflation or hyperinflation has been accompanied by rapid money growth, often to finance government deficits. In the short run the link is loose, because velocity moves with interest rates, financial innovation and confidence, and because output can deviate from potential. This is why central banks focus on interest rates for short-run management while keeping money growth consistent with low inflation over time.

Key takeaway: MV = PY. In the long run, sustained inflation is driven by money growing faster than real output.

modules.title: Monetary policy
modules.summary: How central banks set interest rates, how those rates reach the real economy, and the tools used in crises.

lessons.title: Central bank goals and tools
lessons.summary: Price stability mandates, the policy rate, open market operations and reserve requirements.
lessons.body:
Most central banks have price stability as their main goal, often defined as a numerical inflation target, and many also consider employment and financial stability. Under inflation targeting, the bank publishes its target, explains its decisions and is judged on whether inflation returns to target over a horizon of one to two years. The Central Bank of the Republic of Uzbekistan, like many others, communicates policy mainly through its policy rate (asosiy stavka).

The main tool is the policy interest rate, the rate at which the central bank lends to or takes deposits from commercial banks. To keep short-term market rates close to the policy rate, the central bank uses open market operations (buying or selling government securities, or repo and reverse-repo operations) and a corridor of standing facilities: an overnight lending rate as the ceiling and a deposit rate as the floor.

Other tools include reserve requirements (the share of deposits banks must hold at the central bank), foreign-exchange interventions and macroprudential rules such as limits on loan-to-value ratios. Raising the policy rate is contractionary (tightening) and cutting it is expansionary (easing).

Key takeaway: modern central banks control a short-term interest rate, using open market operations and an interest-rate corridor to make market rates follow the policy rate.

lessons.title: The monetary transmission mechanism
lessons.summary: The channels through which a change in the policy rate affects spending, output and inflation.
lessons.body:
The transmission mechanism describes how a policy rate change reaches the real economy. Suppose the central bank raises its rate by 1 percentage point. First, interbank and short-term market rates rise, and banks raise rates on loans and deposits (the interest-rate channel). Borrowing for homes, cars and business investment becomes more expensive, and saving becomes more attractive, so spending falls.

Other channels reinforce this. Higher domestic rates attract capital and tend to strengthen the currency, which makes imports cheaper and lowers inflation directly (the exchange-rate channel), especially in economies that import much of what they consume. Asset prices such as bonds, shares and property fall, reducing wealth and collateral values (the asset-price and credit channels). Perhaps most importantly, a credible central bank shapes expectations: if firms and workers believe inflation will fall, they set lower prices and wage demands.

Transmission works with long and variable lags. The effect on output typically peaks after around a year and on inflation after one to two years, which is why central banks must act on forecasts rather than current inflation. Transmission is weaker when many loans are in foreign currency, when much credit is directed by the state at subsidized rates, or when financial markets are shallow.

Key takeaway: rate changes work through borrowing costs, the exchange rate, asset prices, credit and expectations, with lags of one to two years. Credibility makes every channel stronger.

lessons.title: The Phillips curve and the Taylor rule
lessons.summary: The short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment and a simple rule for setting interest rates.
lessons.body:
The Phillips curve describes a short-run trade-off: when unemployment is below its natural rate, labor markets are tight and inflation tends to rise; when unemployment is high, inflation tends to fall. The modern, expectations-augmented version is π = πᵉ − β(u − uₙ), where πᵉ is expected inflation. The key lesson of the 1970s was that the trade-off is only temporary: trying to hold unemployment below its natural rate permanently just raises expected inflation, so in the long run the Phillips curve is vertical.

The Taylor rule summarizes how a central bank might set its policy rate: i = r* + π + 0.5 × (π − π*) + 0.5 × (output gap). Here r* is the neutral real interest rate, π is current inflation, π* is the target and the output gap is the percentage difference between actual and potential output. Example: with r* = 2%, π = 8%, π* = 5% and an output gap of +1%, the rule suggests i = 2 + 8 + 1.5 + 0.5 = 12%.

The rule embodies the Taylor principle: when inflation rises by 1 point, the nominal rate should rise by more than 1 point, so that the real interest rate increases and demand cools. Central banks do not follow the rule mechanically, because r* and potential output are uncertain, but it is a useful benchmark for judging whether policy is tight or loose.

Key takeaway: there is a short-run but not a long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment. The Taylor rule says rates should rise more than one-for-one with inflation.

lessons.title: Unconventional policy and credibility
lessons.summary: Quantitative easing, forward guidance and why central bank independence matters.
lessons.body:
When policy rates approach zero, central banks cannot cut them much further; this is the effective lower bound. During the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic, several central banks used unconventional tools. Quantitative easing (QE) means buying large amounts of long-term government bonds and other assets, creating reserves and pushing down long-term interest rates. Forward guidance means committing publicly to keep rates low for a period or until conditions are met, which lowers expectations of future rates and therefore long-term rates today.

Credibility is the foundation of all monetary policy. If people expect the central bank to tolerate high inflation, they build that expectation into wages and prices, and inflation becomes self-fulfilling. Central bank independence, a clear mandate and transparent communication (published targets, forecasts and decision explanations) make it easier to anchor expectations. The opposite case is fiscal dominance: when a central bank is pressured to finance government deficits, money growth and inflation follow.

Example: a central bank that has repeatedly met its target can stop a temporary price shock, such as a rise in fuel prices, from turning into persistent inflation with a modest rate move. A bank with a poor record may need much larger rate increases to achieve the same result.

Key takeaway: at the lower bound, central banks use asset purchases and guidance about future rates. Credibility and independence determine how much any policy move achieves.

measuring-economy.title: Iqtisodiyotni o‘lchash
measuring-economy.summary: YaIM, inflyatsiya va ishsizlik: har qanday makroiqtisodiy munozara boshlanadigan uchta ko‘rsatkich.

ad-as.summary: O‘sish, tanazzul va inflyatsiya uchun yagona tahliliy asos hamda fiskal siyosatning roli.

money-banking.summary: Pul nima, banklar uni qanday yaratadi va pul massasi narxlar bilan qanday bog‘liq.
