multivariable-optimization.summary: Xususiy hosilalar, bir nechta tanlov o‘zgaruvchisi bilan optimallashtirish va cheklovli masalalar uchun Lagranj ko‘paytuvchilari.

derivative-definition.title: Hosila o‘zgarish tezligi sifatida
derivative-definition.summary: Kesuvchi chiziq qiyaligidan oniy o‘zgarish tezligiga qadar.
derivative-definition.body:
Hosila funksiya qanchalik tez o‘zgarishini o‘lchaydi. f funksiyaning x va x + h orasidagi o‘rtacha o‘zgarish tezligi kesuvchi chiziq qiyaligiga teng: [f(x + h) − f(x)] ÷ h. h ni nolga intiltirsak, oniy o‘zgarish tezligi, ya’ni hosila hosil bo‘ladi: f′(x) = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] ÷ h. Geometrik nuqtai nazardan f′(x) — x nuqtadagi urinma chiziqning qiyaligi.

Misol: f(x) = x² uchun [ (x + h)² − x² ] ÷ h = (2xh + h²) ÷ h = 2x + h bo‘lib, h → 0 da 2x ga intiladi. Demak f′(x) = 2x va x = 3 da funksiya resursning har bir birligiga 6 birlik mahsulot tezligida o‘smoqda.

Hosila ishorasi yo‘nalishni ko‘rsatadi: f′(x) > 0 bo‘lsa f o‘suvchi, f′(x) < 0 bo‘lsa kamayuvchi, f′(x) = 0 esa mumkin bo‘lgan cho‘qqi yoki chuqurlikni bildiradi. Differensiallanuvchi bo‘lishi uchun funksiya uzluksiz bo‘lishi shart, lekin uzluksizlik yetarli emas: |x| funksiyasi 0 da uzluksiz, ammo u yerda burchakka ega, shuning uchun yagona urinma qiyaligi mavjud emas.

Asosiy xulosa: hosila o‘rtacha o‘zgarish tezliklarining limitidir. Uning ishorasi funksiya o‘sayotgani yoki kamayayotganini ko‘rsatadi, hosilaning nollari esa optimum nomzodlaridir.

differentiation-rules.title: Differensiallash qoidalari
differentiation-rules.summary: Daraja, ko‘paytma, bo‘linma va murakkab funksiya qoidalari hamda ko‘rsatkichli va logarifmik funksiyalar hosilalari.
differentiation-rules.body:
Har bir hosilani limit ta’rifi orqali hisoblash sekin, shuning uchun qoidalardan foydalanamiz. Daraja qoidasi: d/dx xⁿ = n·xⁿ⁻¹, demak d/dx 3x⁴ = 12x³ va d/dx √x = ½x^(−½). O‘zgarmaslarning hosilasi nolga teng, yig‘indining hosilasi esa hosilalar yig‘indisiga teng. Ko‘paytma qoidasi: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′. Bo‘linma qoidasi: (u ÷ v)′ = (u′v − uv′) ÷ v². Murakkab funksiya (zanjir) qoidasi: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))·g′(x).

Ko‘rsatkichli va logarifmik funksiyalar iqtisodiyotda doimo uchraydi: d/dx eˣ = eˣ, d/dx e^(kx) = k·e^(kx) va d/dx ln x = 1 ÷ x. Yechilgan misollar: ko‘paytma qoidasiga ko‘ra d/dx (x²eˣ) = 2xeˣ + x²eˣ; zanjir qoidasiga ko‘ra d/dx (1 + 2x)⁵ = 5(1 + 2x)⁴ × 2 = 10(1 + 2x)⁴; d/dx ln(5x² + 1) = 10x ÷ (5x² + 1).

Foydali qo‘llanish — o‘sish sur’atlari. Agar o‘zgaruvchi y(t) = y₀e^(gt) ko‘rinishida o‘ssa, d/dt ln y = g, ya’ni uzluksiz o‘sish sur’ati. Umuman olganda, ko‘paytmaning o‘sish sur’ati o‘sish sur’atlarining yig‘indisiga, nisbatning o‘sish sur’ati esa ularning ayirmasiga teng: real YaIM o‘sishi ≈ nominal YaIM o‘sishi − inflyatsiya formulasi logarifmlarni differensiallashdan bevosita kelib chiqadi.

Asosiy xulosa: daraja, ko‘paytma, bo‘linma va zanjir qoidalarini hamda eˣ va ln x hosilalarini puxta o‘zlashtiring; ular birgalikda boshlang‘ich iqtisodiyotdagi deyarli barcha funksiyalarni qamrab oladi.

marginal-cost-revenue.title: Chekli xarajat va chekli daromad hosilalar sifatida
marginal-cost-revenue.summary: Nima uchun iqtisodiyotdagi “chekli” so‘zi matematik tahlildagi “hosila”ni anglatadi.
marginal-cost-revenue.body:
Iqtisodiyotda “chekli” degani bir birlik ko‘proq bo‘lganda umumiy miqdorning o‘zgarishi. Matematik tahlil tilida bu hosila. Agar C(q) umumiy xarajat bo‘lsa, chekli xarajat MC(q) = C′(q). Agar R(q) umumiy tushum bo‘lsa, chekli daromad MR(q) = R′(q), chekli foyda esa π′(q) = R′(q) − C′(q).

Misol: C(q) = 5 000 + 40q + 0,5q². Unda MC(q) = 40 + q, demak q = 100 da chekli xarajat 140 ga teng. 101-birlikning aniq xarajati C(101) − C(100) = 40 + 0,5 × (101² − 100²) = 140,5 bo‘lib, hosilaga juda yaqin. Hosila chiziqli yaqinlashishdir: ΔC ≈ C′(q) × Δq.

Tushum uchun talab P = 200 − 2q bo‘lsin. Unda R(q) = 200q − 2q² va MR(q) = 200 − 4q. q = 30 da MR = 80, narx esa 140: bir birlik ko‘proq sotish uning narxidan kamroq qo‘shadi, chunki firma barcha birliklar narxini tushirishi kerak. MR q = 50 da nolga teng, bu yerda umumiy tushum eng yuqori bo‘ladi va bu nuqta talab egri chizig‘ida birlik elastiklik nuqtasi ham hisoblanadi.

O‘rtacha va chekli miqdorlar bog‘liq: o‘rtacha xarajat AC = C(q) ÷ q MC < AC bo‘lganda kamayadi va MC > AC bo‘lganda oshadi, shuning uchun MC AC ni uning minimum nuqtasida kesib o‘tadi.

Asosiy xulosa: chekli xarajat, daromad va foyda tegishli umumiy miqdorlarning hosilalaridir va hosila yana bir birlikning ta’sirini yaxshi yaqinlashtiradi.

elasticity-calculus.title: Hosilalar yordamida elastiklik
elasticity-calculus.summary: Nuqtaviy elastiklik, doimiy elastiklikka ega funksiyalar va elastiklik bilan tushum o‘rtasidagi bog‘liqlik.
elasticity-calculus.body:
Matematik tahlil elastiklikni aniq nuqtaviy o‘lchovga aylantiradi: E = (dQ/dP) × (P ÷ Q). Bu talab egri chizig‘ining aniq nuqtasida narx 1% ga o‘zgarganda miqdorning foiz o‘zgarishi. Boshqacha aytganda, E = d(ln Q) ÷ d(ln P), ya’ni logarifmik o‘qlardagi talab egri chizig‘ining qiyaligi.

Chiziqli talab misoli: Q = 200 − 4P. P = 20 da Q = 120 va dQ/dP = −4, demak E = −4 × 20 ÷ 120 ≈ −0,67 (noelastik). P = 35 da Q = 60 va E = −4 × 35 ÷ 60 ≈ −2,33 (elastik). To‘g‘ri chiziqli talab egri chizig‘i bo‘ylab qiyalik o‘zgarmas bo‘lsa ham, elastiklik o‘zgaradi.

Doimiy elastiklikka ega talab Q = A·P^(−ε) ko‘rinishida bo‘ladi. Logarifmlasak, ln Q = ln A − ε ln P hosil bo‘ladi, demak elastiklik hamma joyda −ε ga teng. Bu shakl empirik tadqiqotlarda keng qo‘llaniladi, chunki log-log regressiya elastiklikni bevosita baholaydi.

Matematik tahlil tushum qoidasini ham isbotlaydi. R = P·Q(P) bo‘lsa, dR/dP = Q + P·dQ/dP = Q(1 + E). Agar E −1 va 0 orasida bo‘lsa, narxni oshirish tushumni ko‘paytiradi; E < −1 bo‘lsa, kamaytiradi. Miqdor bo‘yicha MR = P(1 + 1 ÷ E) bo‘lib, bu bevosita monopoliya ustamasi qoidasiga olib keladi: (P − MC) ÷ P = −1 ÷ E.

Asosiy xulosa: nuqtaviy elastiklik (dQ/dP)(P/Q) ga teng. dR/dP = Q(1 + E) formulasi narx oshishi qachon tushumni ko‘paytirishini aniq ko‘rsatadi.

critical-points.title: Kritik nuqtalar va ikkinchi hosila testi
critical-points.summary: Maksimum va minimum nomzodlarini toping, so‘ng ularni qavariqlik yordamida tasniflang.
critical-points.body:
Kritik nuqta — f′(x) = 0 yoki f′ mavjud bo‘lmagan nuqta. Ochiq oraliqda differensiallanuvchi funksiyaning har bir lokal maksimumi yoki minimumi kritik nuqtada yuz beradi (birinchi tartibli shart), lekin har bir kritik nuqta optimum emas: f(x) = x³ uchun f′(0) = 0, ammo cho‘qqi ham, chuqurlik ham yo‘q.

Tasniflash uchun ikkinchi hosiladan foydalaning. Agar f′(c) = 0 va f″(c) < 0 bo‘lsa, funksiya c atrofida pastga qavariq va c lokal maksimum. Agar f″(c) > 0 bo‘lsa, funksiya yuqoriga qavariq va c lokal minimum. Agar f″(c) = 0 bo‘lsa, test natija bermaydi va buning o‘rniga f′ ning har ikki tomondagi ishorasini tekshirasiz (birinchi hosila testi).

Misol: f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1. Unda f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), kritik nuqtalar x = 1 va x = 3. f″(x) = 6x − 12 bo‘lgani uchun f″(1) = −6 < 0 lokal maksimum f(1) = 5 ni, f″(3) = 6 > 0 esa lokal minimum f(3) = 1 ni beradi.

Yopiq [a, b] oraliqda global maksimum va minimum f ning barcha kritik nuqtalardagi hamda a va b chegaralardagi qiymatlarini solishtirib topiladi. Iqtisodiyotda qavariqlik ma’noga ega: pastga qavariq foyda funksiyasi kritik nuqta global maksimum ekanini kafolatlaydi.

Asosiy xulosa: nomzodlarni topish uchun f′(x) = 0 deb oling, ularni tasniflash uchun f″ dan foydalaning va soha cheklangan bo‘lsa, chegara nuqtalarni tekshiring.

profit-maximization.title: Foydani maksimallashtirish
profit-maximization.summary: MR = MC qoidasini matematik tahlil orqali keltirib chiqaring va uni bozor hokimiyatiga ega firmaga qo‘llang.
profit-maximization.body:
Foyda — tushum minus xarajat: π(q) = R(q) − C(q). π′(q) = 0 birinchi tartibli sharti R′(q) = C′(q) ni beradi — mashhur chekli daromad = chekli xarajat qoidasi. π″(q) < 0 yoki R″(q) < C″(q) ikkinchi tartibli sharti maksimumni tasdiqlaydi: chekli xarajat chekli daromadni pastdan kesib o‘tishi kerak.

Misol: firma P = 140 − 2q talabiga duch keladi va xarajati C(q) = 100 + 20q + q². Tushum R = 140q − 2q², demak MR = 140 − 4q. Chekli xarajat MC = 20 + 2q. 140 − 4q = 20 + 2q tenglamasi 6q = 120 ni beradi, demak q* = 20 va narx P = 140 − 40 = 100. Foyda R − C = 2 000 − (100 + 400 + 400) = 1 100. π″(q) = −4 − 2 = −6 < 0 bo‘lgani uchun bu maksimumdir.

Amalda ikkita aniqlik muhim. Birinchidan, firma narx o‘rtacha o‘zgaruvchan xarajatni qoplagandagina ishlab chiqarishi kerak; aks holda eng yaxshi hajm nolga teng. Ikkinchidan, doimiy xarajatlar q* ga ta’sir qilmaydi: C(q) dagi 100 ni o‘zgartirish foydani o‘zgartiradi, lekin optimal miqdorni emas, chunki differensiallaganda doimiy xarajatlar yo‘qoladi.

Asosiy xulosa: foydani MR = MC tenglamasini yechib maksimallashtiring, π″ < 0 bilan tasdiqlang va ishlab chiqarish faoliyatni to‘xtatishdan yaxshiroq ekanini tekshiring. Doimiy xarajatlar hech qachon optimal miqdorni o‘zgartirmaydi.

cost-minimization-eoq.title: Xarajatlarni minimallashtirish va optimal buyurtma hajmi
cost-minimization-eoq.summary: Eng arzon zaxira siyosatini topish uchun buyurtma xarajatlarini saqlash xarajatlari bilan muvozanatlang.
cost-minimization-eoq.body:
Ko‘plab biznes masalalari qarama-qarshi yo‘nalishda o‘zgaradigan ikki xarajat o‘rtasida muvozanat izlaydi. Zaxira — klassik misol. Tez-tez buyurtma berish yiliga ko‘p marta har bir buyurtma uchun S doimiy xarajat to‘lashni anglatadi; kam buyurtma berish katta zaxira saqlashni bildiradi, bu esa omborxona, sug‘urta va band bo‘lgan pul uchun har bir birlikka yiliga H xarajat keltiradi.

Yillik talab D va har bir buyurtma hajmi Q bo‘lsa, buyurtmalar soni D ÷ Q, o‘rtacha zaxira esa Q ÷ 2 ga teng. Umumiy yillik xarajat: TC(Q) = (D ÷ Q)·S + (Q ÷ 2)·H. Differensiallaymiz: TC′(Q) = −DS ÷ Q² + H ÷ 2. Uni nolga tenglashtirsak, optimal buyurtma hajmi hosil bo‘ladi: Q* = √(2DS ÷ H). Ikkinchi hosila 2DS ÷ Q³ musbat, demak bu minimum.

Misol: do‘kon yiliga D = 10 000 birlik sotadi, har bir buyurtma yetkazib berish va hujjatlar uchun S = 200 000 so‘m turadi, bir birlikni bir yil saqlash esa H = 4 000 so‘m. Unda Q* = √(2 × 10 000 × 200 000 ÷ 4 000) = √1 000 000 = 1 000 birlik, demak do‘kon yiliga 10 marta buyurtma beradi. Optimal nuqtada yillik buyurtma xarajati (2 000 000 so‘m) yillik saqlash xarajatiga (2 000 000 so‘m) aynan teng.

Xuddi shu mantiq — umumiy xarajat hosilasini nolga tenglashtirish — o‘rtacha xarajatni minimallashtiradigan hajmni, zavoddagi eng yaxshi partiya hajmini yoki yo‘qotilgan foizni pul yechish komissiyalari bilan muvozanatlaydigan naqd pul qoldig‘ini topadi.

Asosiy xulosa: ikki xarajat qarama-qarshi tomonga tortsa, umumiy xarajatni qaror funksiyasi sifatida yozing, differensiallang va hosilani nolga tenglashtiring. Zaxira uchun Q* = √(2DS/H).

partial-derivatives.title: Xususiy hosilalar va chekli mahsulotlar
partial-derivatives.summary: Qolganlarini o‘zgarmas ushlab, bitta o‘zgaruvchi bo‘yicha differensiallash.
partial-derivatives.body:
Iqtisodiy miqdorlar odatda bir nechta o‘zgaruvchiga bog‘liq: mahsulot mehnat va kapitalga, naflilik esa bir nechta tovarga bog‘liq. ∂f/∂x xususiy hosilasi x o‘zgarganda va boshqa barcha o‘zgaruvchilar o‘zgarmas bo‘lganda f qanday o‘zgarishini o‘lchaydi — bu iqtisodchilarning “boshqa sharoitlar teng bo‘lganda” iborasining rasmiy ko‘rinishi. Uni hisoblash uchun boshqa o‘zgaruvchilarni o‘zgarmas deb hisoblang va odatdagidek differensiallang.

Misol: Kobb-Duglas ishlab chiqarish funksiyasi Q = 10·L^0,5·K^0,5. Mehnatning chekli mahsuloti MPL = ∂Q/∂L = 5·L^(−0,5)·K^0,5, kapitalning chekli mahsuloti MPK = ∂Q/∂K = 5·L^0,5·K^(−0,5). L = 25 va K = 100 bo‘lganda mahsulot Q = 10 × 5 × 10 = 500, MPL = 5 × 0,2 × 10 = 10 va MPK = 5 × 5 × 0,1 = 2,5. Har bir xususiy hosila o‘z resursi oshgani sari kamayadi — bu kamayuvchi chekli samaradorlikdir.

Ikkinchi tartibli xususiy hosilalar qo‘shimcha ma’lumot beradi. ∂²Q/∂L² < 0 mehnatning kamayuvchi samaradorligini tasdiqlaydi, aralash hosila ∂²Q/∂L∂K > 0 esa kapital mehnatni unumdorroq qilishini ko‘rsatadi. MPL ÷ MPK nisbati — chekli texnologik almashtirish normasi, ya’ni izokvanta qiyaligi. To‘liq differensial dQ = MPL·dL + MPK·dK ikkala resurs bir vaqtda o‘zgarganda mahsulot o‘zgarishini yaqinlashtiradi.

Asosiy xulosa: xususiy hosila qolganlari o‘zgarmas bo‘lganda bitta o‘zgaruvchining ta’sirini ajratib ko‘rsatadi. Chekli mahsulotlar, chekli nafliliklar va almashtirish normalari — barchasi xususiy hosilalar yoki ularning nisbatlaridir.

unconstrained-multivariable.title: Bir nechta o‘zgaruvchili shartsiz optimallashtirish
unconstrained-multivariable.summary: Har bir xususiy hosilani nolga tenglashtiring va ikkinchi tartibli shartlarni tekshiring; narx diskriminatsiyasiga qo‘llanilishi.
unconstrained-multivariable.body:
f(x, y) ni maksimallashtirish yoki minimallashtirish uchun birinchi tartibli shartlar har bir xususiy hosila nolga teng bo‘lishini talab qiladi: ∂f/∂x = 0 va ∂f/∂y = 0, ya’ni gradient vektori nolga teng. Ikkinchi tartibli shartlar ikkinchi tartibli xususiy hosilalardan iborat Gesse matritsasidan foydalanadi. Ikki o‘zgaruvchili maksimum uchun fₓₓ < 0 va fₓₓ·f_yy − (fₓy)² > 0 bo‘lishi kerak; minimum uchun fₓₓ > 0 va xuddi shu determinant musbat. Agar determinant manfiy bo‘lsa, nuqta egar nuqtasi hisoblanadi.

Misol, uchinchi darajali narx diskriminatsiyasi: firma ikkita alohida bozorda P₁ = 100 − Q₁ va P₂ = 80 − 2Q₂ talablari hamda 20 ga teng doimiy chekli xarajat bilan sotadi. Foyda π = (100 − Q₁)Q₁ + (80 − 2Q₂)Q₂ − 20(Q₁ + Q₂). ∂π/∂Q₁ = 100 − 2Q₁ − 20 = 0 dan Q₁ = 40 va P₁ = 60 kelib chiqadi. ∂π/∂Q₂ = 80 − 4Q₂ − 20 = 0 dan Q₂ = 15 va P₂ = 50 kelib chiqadi. Gesse matritsasining diagonalida −2 va −4, tashqarisida 0 turadi, demak determinant 8 > 0 va πₓₓ < 0, bu maksimumni tasdiqlaydi.

Natija umumiy qoidani ko‘rsatadi: firma har bir bozordagi chekli daromadni chekli xarajatga tenglashtiradi (MR₁ = MR₂ = MC) va talab kamroq elastik bo‘lgan joyda yuqoriroq narx qo‘yadi. Optimal nuqtada elastiklik 1-bozorda taxminan −1,5, 2-bozorda esa −1,67, shuning uchun 1-bozor ko‘proq to‘laydi.

Asosiy xulosa: gradientni nolga tenglashtiring, so‘ng Gesse matritsasini tekshiring. Ko‘p bozorli narx belgilashda bu har bir bozorda MR = MC ni beradi va talab kamroq elastik bo‘lgan joyda narxlar yuqoriroq bo‘ladi.

lagrange-multipliers.title: Lagranj ko‘paytuvchilari: naflilikni maksimallashtirish
lagrange-multipliers.summary: Byudjet yoki resurs cheklovi ostidagi optimallashtirish masalalarini yechish.
lagrange-multipliers.body:
Ko‘plab iqtisodiy masalalar cheklov ostida biror narsani maksimallashtiradi: iste’molchi byudjet doirasida naflilikni, firma xarajat chegarasi doirasida mahsulotni maksimallashtiradi. Lagranj usuli buni hal qiladi. g(x, y) = c sharti ostida f(x, y) ni maksimallashtirish uchun Lagranj funksiyasini tuzamiz: ℒ = f(x, y) + λ[c − g(x, y)] va barcha xususiy hosilalarni nolga tenglashtiramiz: ∂ℒ/∂x = 0, ∂ℒ/∂y = 0 va ∂ℒ/∂λ = 0 (bu shunchaki cheklovni qayta ifodalaydi).

Misol: 10x + 5y = 100 sharti ostida U = x^0,5·y^0,5 ni maksimallashtiring. Shartlar: 0,5·x^(−0,5)·y^0,5 = 10λ, 0,5·x^0,5·y^(−0,5) = 5λ va 10x + 5y = 100. Birinchisini ikkinchisiga bo‘lsak, y ÷ x = 2, demak y = 2x. Byudjetga qo‘yamiz: 10x + 10x = 100, demak x = 5 va y = 10. Naflilik √50 ≈ 7,07.

Dastlabki ikki shart birgalikda MUx ÷ MUy = Px ÷ Py ni bildiradi: befarqlik egri chizig‘ining qiyaligi byudjet chizig‘i qiyaligiga teng, bu iste’molchi nazariyasidagi urinish shartining aynan o‘zi. Kobb-Duglas naflilik funksiyasi U = x^a·y^b uchun yechim har doim daromadning a ÷ (a + b) ulushini x ga va b ÷ (a + b) ulushini y ga sarflaydi, shuning uchun yuqoridagi iste’molchi byudjetning yarmini har bir tovarga sarfladi.

Asosiy xulosa: ℒ = f + λ(c − g) ni tuzing, barcha xususiy hosilalarni nolga tenglashtiring va yeching. Natija har bir so‘mga to‘g‘ri keladigan chekli foyda barcha yo‘nalishlarda teng bo‘lishi kerak degan iqtisodiy qoidani takrorlaydi.

shadow-prices.title: Soya narxlari va xarajatlarni minimallashtirish
shadow-prices.summary: Lagranj ko‘paytuvchisini cheklovni yumshatish qiymati sifatida talqin qiling va maqsadli hajmni ishlab chiqarish xarajatini minimallashtiring.
shadow-prices.body:
Lagranj ko‘paytuvchisi λ kuchli talqinga ega: u cheklov yumshatilganda optimal qiymat o‘zgarish tezligidir, λ = dV*/dc. Naflilik misolida (10x + 5y = 100 sharti bilan x^0,5·y^0,5 ni maksimallashtirish) λ ≈ 0,0707, demak bir so‘m qo‘shimcha daromad maksimal naflilikni taxminan 0,07 ga oshiradi. Shuning uchun λ soya narxi deb ataladi: u o‘z bozor narxiga ega bo‘lmagan resursni, masalan bir soatlik stanok vaqti yoki bir tonna chiqindi kvotasini baholaydi.

Xarajatlarni minimallashtirish mahsulotni maksimallashtirishning ko‘zgudagi aksidir. Firma ish haqi w = 16 va ijara stavkasi r = 4 bo‘lganda Q = L^0,5·K^0,5 = 100 ni minimal wL + rK xarajat bilan ishlab chiqarmoqchi. Birinchi tartibli shartlar MPL ÷ MPK = w ÷ r ni beradi, bu funksiya uchun esa MPL ÷ MPK = K ÷ L, demak K = 4L. Maqsadga qo‘yamiz: L^0,5·(4L)^0,5 = 2L = 100, demak L = 50 va K = 200. Minimal xarajat 16 × 50 + 4 × 200 = 1 600.

Bu yerda λ mahsulotning chekli xarajatidir: yana bir birlik ishlab chiqarish minimal xarajatni λ = 2√(w·r) = 16 ga oshiradi. Bu ishlab chiqarish texnologiyasi, resurs narxlari va firmaning chekli xarajat egri chizig‘i o‘rtasida bevosita bog‘liqlik beradi.

Asosiy xulosa: Lagranj ko‘paytuvchisi qo‘shimcha resursning har bir birligi optimumni qanchalik yaxshilashini ko‘rsatadi. Xarajatlarni minimallashtirishda u chekli xarajatga teng va optimum MPL/MPK = w/r shartini qanoatlantiradi.

topics.title: Probability & Statistics for Data Analysis
topics.description: Reason about uncertainty with probability, model data with distributions, draw conclusions with confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, and measure relationships with regression.

modules.title: Probability foundations
modules.summary: The rules of probability, conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem.

lessons.title: Events and the rules of probability
lessons.summary: Sample spaces, events, complements and the addition rule.
lessons.body:
A random experiment has a sample space S, the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of S. Probabilities follow three axioms: every probability is between 0 and 1, P(S) = 1, and for events that cannot happen together (mutually exclusive events) probabilities add. When all outcomes are equally likely, P(A) = number of outcomes in A ÷ number of outcomes in S.

Three rules follow. The complement rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A), which is often the easiest route, as in P(at least one success) = 1 − P(no successes). The addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); the subtraction prevents double-counting outcomes in both events. For mutually exclusive events, P(A and B) = 0.

Example: in a survey of 500 shoppers, 300 use a mobile banking app, 200 use a card, and 120 use both. The probability that a random shopper uses at least one is P(app or card) = 300/500 + 200/500 − 120/500 = 380/500 = 0.76, and the probability of using neither is 1 − 0.76 = 0.24.

Key takeaway: list the sample space clearly, use the complement rule for “at least one” questions, and subtract the overlap when adding probabilities of events that can occur together.

lessons.title: Conditional probability and independence
lessons.summary: How new information changes probabilities, and what it means for events to be independent.
lessons.body:
Conditional probability is the probability of A given that B has happened: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Knowing B restricts attention to the outcomes inside B. Rearranging gives the multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A | B) × P(B).

Events are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other: P(A | B) = P(A), or equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are never independent: if one happens, the other certainly does not.

Example: an online store finds that 40% of visitors are returning customers, and 15% of all visitors are returning customers who buy. Given that a visitor is returning, the probability of a purchase is 0.15 ÷ 0.40 = 0.375. If 20% of all visitors buy, then returning visitors are far more likely to buy than average (37.5% versus 20%), so “returning” and “buys” are not independent.

A two-way table of counts makes these calculations concrete: divide a cell by its row total for one conditional probability and by its column total for the other. Be careful not to confuse P(A | B) with P(B | A); they are usually very different, which is the topic of Bayes’ theorem.

Key takeaway: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Independence means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B), and should be checked rather than assumed.

lessons.title: Bayes’ theorem
lessons.summary: Update beliefs with evidence, and avoid the base-rate fallacy.
lessons.body:
Bayes’ theorem reverses a conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) ÷ P(B), where the denominator can be expanded with the law of total probability as P(B) = P(B | A)P(A) + P(B | not A)P(not A). P(A) is the prior, P(B | A) the likelihood, and P(A | B) the posterior: the updated belief after seeing evidence B.

Example: 1% of card transactions are fraudulent. A detection system flags 95% of fraudulent transactions but also wrongly flags 5% of legitimate ones. If a transaction is flagged, what is the probability it is really fraud? P(flag) = 0.95 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059. So P(fraud | flag) = 0.0095 ÷ 0.059 ≈ 0.16. Only about 16% of flagged transactions are fraudulent.

The surprise comes from the low base rate. Because legitimate transactions vastly outnumber fraudulent ones, even a small false-positive rate produces many more false alarms than true detections. Ignoring the prior is called the base-rate fallacy, and it appears in medical testing, credit scoring, spam filtering and hiring.

A practical trick is natural frequencies: imagine 10,000 transactions. 100 are fraud and 95 of those are flagged; 9,900 are legitimate and 495 of those are flagged. Of 590 flags, 95 are fraud, about 16%.

Key takeaway: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. When the base rate is low, a positive signal can still leave the event unlikely.

modules.title: Random variables and distributions
modules.summary: Expected value and variance, the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions, and the central limit theorem.

lessons.title: Expected value, variance and standard deviation
lessons.summary: Summarize a random variable by its long-run average and its spread.
lessons.body:
A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. For a discrete random variable, the expected value is the probability-weighted average of its values: E[X] = Σ x·P(X = x). It is the long-run average if the experiment were repeated many times. Variance measures spread around the mean: Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])², and the standard deviation is σ = √Var(X), in the same units as X.

Example: a small investment pays a profit of 200 with probability 0.3, 50 with probability 0.5, and a loss of 100 with probability 0.2 (in thousands of UZS). E[X] = 200(0.3) + 50(0.5) − 100(0.2) = 60 + 25 − 20 = 65. E[X²] = 40,000(0.3) + 2,500(0.5) + 10,000(0.2) = 15,250, so Var(X) = 15,250 − 65² = 11,025 and σ = 105. The investment has a positive expected return but large risk relative to it.

Useful rules: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X). Expectations always add: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]. Variances add only for independent (or uncorrelated) variables; in general Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y). Diversification works because combining assets that are not perfectly correlated reduces variance relative to expected return.

Key takeaway: the expected value is the centre and the standard deviation is the typical distance from it. In finance, these become expected return and risk.

lessons.title: Binomial and Poisson distributions
lessons.summary: Models for counting successes in fixed trials and events in a fixed interval.
lessons.body:
The binomial distribution counts the number of successes X in n independent trials, each with the same success probability p. Its probability formula is P(X = k) = C(n, k)·pᵏ·(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, where C(n, k) = n! ÷ [k!(n − k)!] counts the ways to choose which trials succeed. Its mean is np and its variance np(1 − p).

Example: 20% of website visitors sign up for a newsletter. Among 10 visitors, the probability that exactly 2 sign up is C(10, 2)(0.2)²(0.8)⁸ = 45 × 0.04 × 0.1678 ≈ 0.302. The expected number is 10 × 0.2 = 2, with variance 1.6.

The Poisson distribution counts events occurring randomly in a fixed interval of time or space at an average rate λ: P(X = k) = e^(−λ)·λᵏ ÷ k!. Its mean and variance both equal λ. It models customer arrivals, support tickets per hour, defects per metre of fabric or claims per month. Example: a call centre receives on average λ = 3 calls per minute. The probability of no calls in a given minute is e^(−3) ≈ 0.050, and of exactly 2 calls is e^(−3) × 9 ÷ 2 ≈ 0.224.

The Poisson distribution approximates the binomial when n is large and p small, with λ = np. Both distributions assume independence; if events cluster, such as calls surging after an outage, the models understate variability.

Key takeaway: use the binomial for successes out of a fixed number of trials, and the Poisson for counts of events at a constant average rate.

lessons.title: The normal distribution
lessons.summary: The bell curve, z-scores and the 68–95–99.7 rule.
lessons.body:
The normal distribution is the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. Many measurements, such as heights, measurement errors and averages of many small effects, are approximately normal. For continuous variables, probabilities are areas under the density curve, so P(X = x) for a single value is zero and we ask about intervals instead.

Any normal variable can be standardized with a z-score: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ, the number of standard deviations x lies from the mean. The standard normal distribution has μ = 0 and σ = 1, and its probabilities come from tables or software. The empirical rule gives quick estimates: about 68% of values lie within 1σ of the mean, 95% within 2σ (more precisely 1.96σ) and 99.7% within 3σ.

Example: delivery times for a courier are normal with μ = 30 minutes and σ = 5 minutes. The probability that a delivery takes over 40 minutes is P(Z > (40 − 30) ÷ 5) = P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.023, about 1 in 44. To promise delivery on time 95% of the time (one-sided), set the promise at μ + 1.645σ ≈ 38.2 minutes.

Many real-world variables are not normal. Incomes, firm sizes and financial returns are often skewed or have fat tails, where extreme values occur far more often than the normal model predicts. Always plot the data before assuming normality.

Key takeaway: convert to z-scores to find normal probabilities, and use 68–95–99.7 as a mental check. Do not assume normality for skewed or fat-tailed data.

lessons.title: Sampling distributions and the central limit theorem
lessons.summary: Why sample means are approximately normal and how precision grows with sample size.
lessons.body:
A statistic such as the sample mean x̄ varies from sample to sample. Its probability distribution across all possible samples is the sampling distribution. If observations are independent with mean μ and standard deviation σ, then E[x̄] = μ (the sample mean is unbiased) and its standard deviation, called the standard error, is SE = σ ÷ √n.

The central limit theorem (CLT) states that for large enough n, the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the original population. A common rule of thumb is n ≥ 30, though strongly skewed data need more. This is why normal-based methods work for averages and proportions even when individual data are not normal.

Example: daily spending per customer has μ = 60,000 UZS and σ = 24,000 UZS and is right-skewed. For samples of n = 36 customers, x̄ is approximately normal with mean 60,000 and SE = 24,000 ÷ 6 = 4,000. The probability that a sample average exceeds 68,000 is P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.023.

Because SE shrinks with √n, precision has diminishing returns: to halve the standard error you need four times as many observations. For a proportion p, the standard error is √[p(1 − p) ÷ n], which is the basis of the margin of error in opinion polls.

Key takeaway: sample means are centred on μ with standard error σ/√n and are approximately normal for large n. Quadrupling the sample halves the error.

modules.title: Statistical inference
modules.summary: Estimate unknown quantities with confidence intervals and test claims with hypothesis tests and A/B experiments.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals
lessons.summary: Report an estimate together with its uncertainty.
lessons.body:
A point estimate such as a sample mean is almost never exactly right, so we report a confidence interval: estimate ± critical value × standard error. For a mean with a large sample, a 95% interval is x̄ ± 1.96 × s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation. For small samples from roughly normal data, the critical value comes from the t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, which is wider than 1.96.

Example: a survey of n = 100 customers finds average monthly spending x̄ = 85,000 UZS with s = 20,000 UZS. SE = 20,000 ÷ 10 = 2,000, and the 95% confidence interval is 85,000 ± 1.96 × 2,000 = 85,000 ± 3,920, or about 81,100 to 88,900 UZS. For a proportion, use p̂ ± 1.96√[p̂(1 − p̂) ÷ n]: if 240 of 400 respondents prefer a product, p̂ = 0.60 and the interval is 0.60 ± 0.048.

Interpretation matters. A 95% confidence level means that if we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value. It does not mean there is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains it. Wider intervals come from higher confidence levels, more variable data or smaller samples. To cut the margin of error in half, you need four times the sample size.

Key takeaway: always report estimates with an interval: estimate ± critical value × SE. The interval reflects sampling error only, not biased samples or bad measurement.

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing and p-values
lessons.summary: Null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values and the two types of error.
lessons.body:
A hypothesis test asks whether data provide enough evidence against a default claim. The null hypothesis H₀ is the status quo (for example, the mean fill weight is 500 g); the alternative H₁ is what we look for evidence of (the mean is not 500 g). We compute a test statistic measuring how far the data are from H₀ in standard-error units, z or t = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ SE, and then the p-value: the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of results at least as extreme as those observed.

Example: a factory claims bags contain 500 g. A sample of n = 49 bags has x̄ = 497 g and s = 7 g. SE = 7 ÷ 7 = 1, so t ≈ (497 − 500) ÷ 1 = −3. The two-sided p-value is about 0.004. At the usual significance level α = 0.05, p < α, so we reject H₀: the evidence suggests bags are underfilled.

Two errors are possible. A Type I error rejects a true H₀ (a false alarm), and its probability is α. A Type II error fails to reject a false H₀ (a missed effect), with probability β; the power of a test is 1 − β. Larger samples increase power. A p-value is not the probability that H₀ is true, and “fail to reject” is not proof that H₀ is true; it means the evidence was insufficient.

Key takeaway: state H₀ and H₁ before looking at the data, compute the test statistic and p-value, and compare with α. Report the effect size and a confidence interval alongside the p-value.

lessons.title: Comparing two groups: A/B testing
lessons.summary: Test whether a change really improved a conversion rate using a two-proportion z-test.
lessons.body:
An A/B test randomly assigns users to a control version (A) and a variant (B) and compares an outcome such as the conversion rate. Randomization is what allows a causal conclusion: apart from chance, the only systematic difference between the groups is the change being tested.

For conversion rates, use the two-proportion z-test. With pooled proportion p = (x_A + x_B) ÷ (n_A + n_B), the standard error is SE = √[p(1 − p)(1/n_A + 1/n_B)] and z = (p̂_B − p̂_A) ÷ SE.

Example: version A converts 200 of 4,000 visitors (5.0%); version B converts 260 of 4,000 (6.5%). The pooled rate is 460 ÷ 8,000 = 5.75%, so SE = √[0.0575 × 0.9425 × (2 ÷ 4,000)] ≈ 0.0052. Then z = 0.015 ÷ 0.0052 ≈ 2.88 and the two-sided p-value is about 0.004. The lift of 1.5 percentage points (30% relative) is statistically significant at α = 0.05, and a 95% interval for the difference is roughly 0.5 to 2.5 points.

Good practice: decide the sample size in advance using a power calculation for the smallest effect worth detecting; do not stop the test early the moment p dips below 0.05 (“peeking” inflates false positives); run the test over full weekly cycles; and check that the split of users between groups matches the design.

Key takeaway: randomize, fix the sample size in advance, and use a two-proportion z-test. Report the lift with a confidence interval, not just “significant”.

lessons.title: Pitfalls: multiple testing and practical significance
lessons.summary: Why many tests produce false discoveries and why statistically significant does not mean important.
lessons.body:
If you run one test at α = 0.05 when there is no real effect, the chance of a false positive is 5%. If you run 20 independent tests, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64%. Testing many metrics, segments or variants and reporting only the significant ones (sometimes called p-hacking or data dredging) almost guarantees spurious findings. Remedies include pre-registering a primary metric, the Bonferroni correction (use α ÷ m for m tests, so 0.0025 for 20 tests) and confirming surprising results with a fresh sample.

Statistical significance is also not the same as practical importance. With a huge sample, a difference of 0.01 percentage points in conversion can be highly significant yet worthless commercially. With a small sample, an important effect may fail to reach significance. Always look at the effect size and its confidence interval, and ask whether the change would matter for decisions, revenue or welfare.

Other common traps: selection bias (analysing only customers who stayed), survivorship bias (studying only successful firms), Simpson’s paradox (a trend that reverses when data are split into groups), and regression to the mean (extreme results tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, which can make an intervention look effective when it was not).

Key takeaway: limit and pre-specify your tests, correct for multiple comparisons, and judge results by effect size and confidence intervals, not by p-values alone.

modules.title: Correlation and regression
modules.summary: Measure and model relationships between variables, and know when a relationship is causal.

lessons.title: Covariance and correlation
lessons.summary: Measure the strength and direction of a linear relationship.
lessons.body:
Covariance measures whether two variables move together: Cov(X, Y) = average of (x − x̄)(y − ȳ). It is positive when above-average x tends to come with above-average y, and negative when they move in opposite directions. Its size depends on the units, so it is hard to interpret on its own.

The correlation coefficient standardizes covariance: r = Cov(X, Y) ÷ (s_X·s_Y). It always lies between −1 and +1. Values near +1 or −1 indicate a strong linear relationship; values near 0 indicate little linear relationship. r is unit-free, symmetric in X and Y, and unaffected by changing units, for example from som to dollars.

Three warnings. First, correlation measures only linear association: a perfect U-shaped relationship can have r = 0, so always plot a scatter diagram. Second, a few outliers can create or destroy a correlation. Third, and most important, correlation is not causation. Ice-cream sales and drowning incidents are correlated because both rise in hot weather, a confounding variable. Cities with more police often have more crime, partly because more police are sent where crime is high, which is reverse causality.

Key takeaway: r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship on a scale from −1 to 1. Plot the data, watch for outliers, and never read causation from correlation alone.

lessons.title: Simple linear regression
lessons.summary: Fit a line by least squares, interpret its slope, and measure fit with R².
lessons.body:
Simple linear regression models y as a straight-line function of x plus an error: y = a + b·x + e. Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses a and b to minimize the sum of squared residuals, where a residual is the gap between an actual and a predicted value. The solution is b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)² and a = ȳ − b·x̄, so the fitted line always passes through the point of means.

Example: advertising spend x (million UZS) and sales y (million UZS) for five months are (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 7), (5, 8). Here x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 5.4. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 12 and Σ(x − x̄)² = 10, so b = 1.2 and a = 5.4 − 1.2 × 3 = 1.8. The fitted line is ŷ = 1.8 + 1.2x: each extra million UZS of advertising is associated with 1.2 million UZS more sales.

R², the coefficient of determination, is the share of the variation in y explained by the line: R² = 1 − (sum of squared residuals ÷ total sum of squares). Here the total sum of squares is 17.2 and the explained part is 14.4, so R² ≈ 0.84. For simple regression, R² = r².

Before trusting the fit, examine the residuals: they should show no pattern against x, have roughly constant spread and contain no extreme outliers. A standard error for b gives a confidence interval and a t-test of whether the true slope is zero. Predictions far outside the observed range of x (extrapolation) are unreliable.

Key takeaway: OLS gives b = Cov(x, y)/Var(x) and a = ȳ − b·x̄. Interpret the slope as the change in y associated with a one-unit change in x, and check residuals before relying on it.

lessons.title: Multiple regression and causal inference
lessons.summary: Control for several factors at once, interpret coefficients correctly, and recognise omitted-variable bias.
lessons.body:
Multiple regression includes several explanatory variables: y = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … + e. Each coefficient bⱼ measures the association between xⱼ and y holding the other included variables constant. For example, in a wage regression with years of education and years of experience, the education coefficient compares people with the same experience.

Useful specifications: dummy variables (0/1) capture categories such as region or gender; a log-log model, ln y = b₀ + b₁ ln x, makes b₁ an elasticity; and a log-level model, ln y = b₀ + b₁x, means a one-unit increase in x changes y by roughly 100·b₁ percent. Adjusted R² penalizes adding variables that do not improve fit.

The main threat to interpretation is omitted-variable bias. If a variable that affects y and is correlated with an included x is left out, the coefficient on x absorbs its effect. Returns to education are overstated if ability is omitted, because more able people tend to get more education and also earn more. Multicollinearity, when explanatory variables are highly correlated with each other, does not bias coefficients but makes them imprecise.

To move from association to causation, economists rely on research designs: randomized experiments, natural experiments, difference-in-differences (comparing changes over time between treated and untreated groups), instrumental variables and regression discontinuity. Each replaces “as if random” variation for the unavailable experiment.

Key takeaway: a multiple regression coefficient is a partial effect holding other included variables fixed. Without a credible research design, omitted variables can make it a correlation, not a causal effect.
